extracted.intended_audience: learned readers of natural theology, philosophers, anatomists, and students of physiology interested in arguments from design
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and using anatomical, physiological, and observational facts about the senses (hearing, taste, smell, touch) to argue for purposeful design rather than chance; includes recommended experiments, analogies, and appeals to authority to support teleological conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure-and-use implies design (teleological inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When he contemplates the Instruments of Hearing so necessary to all Men living, and the great Number of them, ... let him ask himself whether ... he could suppose a Man ... to be the Inventer thereof ... whether it be not the Fear of being forced to own an Adorable and Powerful Creator which restrains him, rather than the true Evidence of his own Mind; ... would he presume to ascribe their Structure, when he observes their Uses, to Chance or ignorant Causes, and conclude that it was to these they owed their Original?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the tight fit between anatomical structure and function (e.g. ear, tympanum, nerves) as positive evidence of contrivance; weigh observed uses alongside structure before invoking chance. (Example/analogy: rigging on a ship cannot reasonably be ascribed to chance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility test: could a human inventor plausibly explain it?
rubrics_metrics.description: let him, in order to come to a sounder Mind, ask himself, whether if he could with any Shew of Reason suppose a Man, from whom he had nothing to fear, to be the Inventer thereof, he could not, with much less Scruple ... impute the Wisdom of such an Invention to such a Man, than to fortuitous and ignorant Causes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the counterfactual question 'could a human plausibly have invented this?' as a quick plausibility probe: if not, favor inference to design. This is a rhetorical diagnostic rather than a formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional fit to environment as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Instruments of Hearing are unnecessary without Air: As the Eye without Light, so this wonderful Structure of the Instruments of Hearing would be in a manner useless, if he ... had not vouchsafed to encompass that Globe ... with a vast Ocean of Air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a sensory organ's form is specially adapted to the medium it operates in (e.g. ear paired with air). Close match between medium and organ strengthens teleological conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attribute contrivance to chance when uses are evident
rubrics_metrics.description: And yet would he presume to ascribe their Structure, when he observes their Uses, to Chance or ignorant Causes, and conclude that it was to these they owed their Original?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an anti-pattern, avoid simplistic appeals to 'chance' to explain well-matched structure and function. Instead seek causal accounts that can account for the evident utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual precision: distinguish sonus primus and sonus secundus
rubrics_metrics.description: It is obvious that all we Hear is only a Kind of Sound ... by Sound a twofold Thing is commonly understood: First, A Motion in the Bodies from whence Sound arises ... called by the Learned, Sonus Primus. Secondly, that Sensation produced in us by such a Motion ... called Sonus Secundus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about sound, clearly separate physical motion (external vibrations) from the internal sensation/perception; failure to maintain this distinction muddles argument and experiment interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple experiments to test seat and mechanism of senses
rubrics_metrics.description: A little powdered Sugar ... lay it upon the Tongue ... as soon as ever they are melted, he will begin to taste ... if he presses it with the Tongue against the hinder Part of the Palate ... he will plainly find, that that Part is likewise affected with the Sweetness. ... one that holds his Breath, though never so little, can easily experience ... he is not affected with it, till he draws in his Breath again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform straightforward, repeatable experiments (e.g., sugar on tongue/palate; holding breath for smell) to localize sensory function and test mechanistic claims rather than relying solely on speculation or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical connections corroborate function (use authorities carefully)
rubrics_metrics.description: This little Nervous Body ... runs across the Drum-Membrane ... Chorda Tympani ... Monſieur du Verney has irrefragably proved, that this nervous Cord is a Branch of the Fifth Pair ... Valsalva ... Malpighi ... the Nerves of the Fifth and Ninth Pair ... are inserted in these Papillæ ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anatomical detail and expert descriptions (Valſalva, du Verney, Malpighi, etc.) to support functional inferences, but acknowledge disagreements among anatomists and seek corroborating experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as a heuristic for improbability of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Will any one dare to maintain, if he saw a Ship sailing with all its Tackle, that the Ropes, Sails, Pullies ... are put into such a State by mere Chance, or without Design; and yet that every one of them was very useful in causing the Ship to move? And is it not more unreasonable to assert the same of these wonderful Things ... ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear analogies (e.g., ship rigging) to illustrate why highly integrated, functional systems are unlikely to be the product of mere chance. Analogies are rhetorical and heuristic, not formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experiential/clinical instances to show sensory effects on passions
rubrics_metrics.description: We find a Relation of a great Musician ... taken with a continued Fever and great Ravings ... both of them were perfectly restored to their Senses by Music. ... Persons stung by a Tarantula ... this great Evil ... can only be cured by the Sound of Music ... sudden Variations in Tunes ... do produce strange Effects upon our Minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and cite empirical cases (medical, anecdotal, historical) showing that sounds/music and other noises evoke or cure passions and disorders; use such cases to demonstrate the causal potency of auditory stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing's special properties: representing absent things and exciting passions
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Hearing, among all the Senses, should have the Faculty to represent to the Mind absent Things, either future or past, by the Means of the Sound of Words ... That the Instruments belonging to the Sense of Hearing ... are enabled to excite all our Passions and Inclinations, and to awake the Powers of our Minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for the special role of hearing, emphasize two properties: (1) capacity to represent absent things via language, and (2) structural propensity to excite passions. These properties explain hearing's unique cultural/spiritual role (e.g., propagation of faith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of multiple physiological mechanisms in causal explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Motions of the Dura Mater, which encompasses the Nerves, do likewise contribute to the producing these Passions and Emotions ... the Nerves of the Eighth Pair ... encompass those of the Fifth Pair ... the Auditory Nerves rise close to the Root of the Eighth ... there is such a great Sympathy between the Ear and the Bowels ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build causal accounts that integrate nerve branches, membranes (dura mater), and sympathetic relations (fifth/eighth pairs) rather than isolating single organs; show how combined effects produce emotions and bodily responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical placement must serve functional purpose (taste and smell examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seat of Tasting is in the Mouth ... Malpighi has discovered Papillæ in the Palate ... the Instruments of Smelling are to be found exactly in the Place through which the Air continually passes and repasses on the Account of Respiration ... the Nostrils are broader at the Bottom ... but narrower at the Top ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that anatomical location (tongue, palate, top of nostrils) matches the sensory function (ingestion for taste, air passage for smell); such spatial-functional correspondences support design inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experiment and experience to doctrinal speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Since this is a thing in which Experience, as in all others, ought to be the Judge ... this Experiment seemed indeed too trifling and too well known to be mentioned here ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputes among theorists arise, defer to reproducible experience and simple experiments to adjudicate claims about sensory mechanisms and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh expert disagreement and admit uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning the right Use of this little Nerve the Opinions of the Anatomists are various, all of them looking upon it as a thing sufficiently obscure ... Fallopius, says he, was uncertain what it was; Eustachius takes it for a Branch of the Nerves of the Fourth Pair; ... Monſieur du Verney has irrefragably proved ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record divergent authoritative views and avoid overconfidence; present multiple expert positions and note where further investigation is required before drawing firm conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physiological properties to argue higher (theological) ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering that the Great God ... has thought fit to propagate Saving Faith in his adorable Son by the Means of Hearing ... it seemed to me ... for these Reasons, that the Instruments of Hearing have received such a different Contexture from those of all the other Senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing sensory facts in theological argument, connect physiological properties to proposed higher purposes (e.g., hearing's suitability to convey words and stir the passions as means for spiritual ends), but make explicit the inferential bridge from biology to theology.
